abo.def: The blood group system set by sugars added to the H antigen on red cells: type A carries the A antigen, type B the B antigen, type AB both, type O neither. From infancy, plasma holds antibodies against whichever of A and B the red cells lack.

agglutination.def: The clumping of cells when antibodies, each with two or more binding sites, bind antigens on several cells and cross-link them. It is an immune process, not clotting, and is often followed by hemolysis.

rh-factor.def: The D antigen, a red cell membrane protein. Rh-positive red cells carry it; Rh-negative cells do not. Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure to Rh-positive cells, through transfusion or pregnancy.

transfusion-reaction.def: Harm caused by a transfusion; the most dangerous is the recipient's antibodies attacking ABO-incompatible donor red cells, causing agglutination, hemolysis, fever, dark urine, low blood pressure and kidney damage. O negative red cells are the universal donor, AB positive the universal recipient, and a crossmatch mixes the patient's plasma with the donor's cells to check before transfusion.

hdn.def: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis): a mother's antibodies cross to the fetus and destroy its red cells. The severe form occurs when an Rh-negative mother, sensitized by an earlier Rh-positive baby, makes anti-D that attacks a later Rh-positive fetus; anti-D immune globulin prevents it.
